claim: Lee, following Kullmann and Siepmann, describes LOTR's narrator as omnipresent and heterodiegetic, less intrusive than The Hobbit's, ranging over the battlefield with the Old English poet's freedom from space and time.
source: Lee 2022, close reading (ORA PDF)

verdict.trueWording: does not take part in the story
verdict.note: Verbatim: 'we get a "heterodiegetic" narrator who does not take part in the story (Kullmann and Siepmann, 2021, 90)'. Every element checks out: 'Whilst not as intrusive as we find in The Hobbit... the narrator takes on an omnipresent role moving back and forth across Middle-earth'; 'the narrative swoops across the battlefield like a drone'; and footnote 21 supplies the Old English poet element — 'Described famously by Renoir (1962) as the Old English poet's ability to be free of "space and time", akin to a film director.' claim: Rosebury shows Tolkien favouring plain descriptive phrasal verbs 'have on' and 'get off' over the more literary 'wear' and 'dismount', and rejects unsupported charges of archaising and wrenched syntax.
source: Wikipedia, 'Tolkien: A Cultural Phenomenon'
quote: a certain sensuous precision, distinctive of Tolkien

verdict.trueWording: familiar phrasal verbs 'have on' and 'get off'
verdict.note: Substance confirmed, but the supplied quote is a decoy. The supporting passage: 'Allan Turner comments in the same work that Rosebury rejects the unsupported assertions of archaising and "wrenched syntax" by critics like Catharine Stimpson, and that Rosebury pointed out that Tolkien used a plain descriptive style, demonstrably favouring the "familiar phrasal verbs 'have on' and 'get off' .. to the slightly more literary 'wear' and 'dismount'".' The quoted phrase 'a certain sensuous precision, distinctive of Tolkien' DOES appear verbatim on the page, but in an unrelated passage several paragraphs earlier — Nancy-Lou Patterson in Mythlore liking Rosebury's characterisation of 'Tolkien's descriptive gifts'. It is not evidence for the phrasal-verb claim; the citation should be repointed to the Turner sentence.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the supplied quote 'a certain sensuous precision' - it sits in an unrelated Mythlore passage and is not evidence for the phrasal-verb claim

claim: Simon's lesson for fantasy writers is that stylistic choices must serve the story and never call attention to themselves, or they bounce the reader out.
source: Tom Simon, The rhetoric of Middle-earth (Bondwine, 2013-01-11)
quote: bouncing one out of the story

verdict.trueWording: This is what is meant by the expression 'bouncing one out of the story'
verdict.note: Quotation verbatim, and the lesson is on the page: 'Our grave danger as writers, then, is that we will do something to wrench the reader's attention away from the story and back to the text... we need to keep their minds on the story as much as possible, which generally means keeping it off the text.' One nuance: Simon does not counsel plain invisibility - he explicitly rejects flat prose as 'too flat to engage the emotions' and argues for a broad emotional range, so 'never call attention to themselves' should be read as 'never wrench attention from story to text'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'never call attention to themselves' - Simon explicitly rejects flat prose and argues for a broad emotional range

Purpose limb verbatim: 'to suggest not just the past, but a whole past speech community'. But the post frames these as 'the remaining 6' of an eleven-item list continued from the previous week (which covered 'here be dragons', 'unsavoury louts they were', 'prithee'), so the six are not the whole taxonomy the claim implies.

claim: A commenter notes the Nazgûl uses thee/thou while Éowyn answers in modern 'you', and that Tolkien was very deliberate about when he used 'thou'.
source: The 'Ye Olde' in Epic Fantasy: 6 More Archaisms (Thoughts on Fantasy)
quote: very deliberate about when he used 'thou'

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that one commenter made both observations - they are two different commenters
verdict.trueWording: Ksenia on Eowyn's 'you'; bdandmcfoster on Tolkien's deliberate 'thou'
verdict.note: Both observations are in the comment thread, but by different people. Ksenia (21 Aug 2019): 'notice that Eowyn herself doesn't say "thee" or "thy", she just says "you."' bdandmcfoster (16 Sep 2020): 'Tolkien was very deliberate about when he used "thou" and when he used "you", and explains this in, I think, one of the appendices.' Quote is word-for-word (page uses curly double quotes around thou). The article body separately quotes the Nazgul's thee/thy speech to Eowyn.

claim: My Tolkien Archive judges the parody mimics the forms (foreword, map, prologue) with lazy names, without genuine engagement with Tolkien's prose itself.
source: Bored of the Rings: A Parody (My Tolkien Archive)

verdict.trueWording: spends a lot of time imitating the forms of it
verdict.note: mytolkienarchive.wordpress.com raw page. Supported: 'It certainly spends a lot of time imitating the forms of it' (cover art, the authors' statement mimicking Tolkien's Ace-paperback response, 'to the maps, the most basic story and overall shape of things') and the lazy-names limb ('Dildo Buggers! Really? That's the best you could come up with? ... Lazy.'). NOT supported: the review never discusses Tolkien's prose; its complaint is absence of affection/appreciation ('it never really feels like there's any affection there'; 'any hint that they actually appreciate the original work as anything other than a platform'). 'Foreword' appears nowhere on the page; 'prologue' appears only inside the page's blockquoted Wikipedia summary, not in the reviewer's own judgement.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: no genuine engagement with Tolkien's prose itself - the review never mentions prose (its charge is lack of affection); 'foreword' is absent from the page and 'prologue' occurs only in the quoted Wikipedia blurb

claim: Shalizi's review frames the Guide as an attack on fifty years of trilogies that are debased versions of The Lord of the Rings, which Jones calls elf operas.
source: Diana Wynne Jones, The Tough Guide to Fantasyland (Cosma Shalizi review)
quote: elf operas

verdict.trueWording: 'elf operas,' as they were recently named on Usenet
verdict.note: bactra.org raw page. Quote 'elf operas' present, and the fifty-years/debased-trilogies limb is verbatim: 'it is still, fifty years on, churning out trilogies which are debased versions of The Lord of the Rings --- ``elf operas,'' as they were recently named on Usenet.' But Shalizi credits the coinage to Usenet, not to Jones; Jones is credited only with 'an open, flagrant and ... hilarious parody'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: which Jones calls elf operas - Shalizi attributes the term to Usenet ('as they were recently named on Usenet'), not to Jones

claim: The production set many poems to music, with Bill Nighy singing the fall of Gil-galad and Bilbo's Last Song and Douglas Livingstone reciting the Khazad-dûm poem.
source: Review: The BBC Lord of the Rings Dramatization (Tolkien Library)

verdict.trueWording: Nighy sings Gil-galad; Le Mesurier sings Bilbo's Last Song
verdict.note: Verified: 'putting many of the poems and songs to music'; 'William Nighy as Sam singing a part of the fall of Gil-Galad'; 'Douglas Livingstone does a splendid job with Gimli's Khazad-dum poem'. But the page attributes Bilbo's Last Song to John Le Mesurier ('a demo version of John Le Mesurier singing Bilbo's Last Song'); its own sentence names Nighy's second song as 'his song in the tower of Minas Morgul', not Bilbo's Last Song.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that Bill Nighy sings Bilbo's Last Song - the page credits John Le Mesurier

claim: Sibley's own page credits Gerard Murphy with the series' strong narrative voice, notes Christopher Tolkien's pronunciation cassette, and concedes that Tolkien's interlaced chronology could not be applied to a dramatic presentation.
source: Brian Sibley: The Works — The Lord of the Rings (BBC Radio 1981)

verdict.trueWording: Tolkien wanted the threads NOT interwoven but on individual chronology
verdict.note: Verified on Sibley's blog: 'Gerard Murphy, who gave the series its strong narrative voice'; Christopher Tolkien's help 'included recording an audiocassette of the acceptable pronunciation of Middle-earth words and names'. But the chronology sentence reads: Tolkien 'had been adamant that the two main threads ... should not be interwoven, but should follow their own individual chronology, as they do in the book', which Sibley concluded could not 'be applied to a dramatic presentation'. The page's word is un-interwoven/individual, the opposite of the claim's 'interlaced'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: calling the chronology Sibley rejected 'interlaced' - the page says Tolkien insisted the threads NOT be interwoven, each on its own chronology

claim: Series One, which cut scenes, was welcomed (appreciation 64/100); Series Two, which compressed them, was heard as a footling and ridiculous-sounding adventure story.
source: The Lord of the Rings (1955 radio series) (Wikipedia)

verdict.trueWording: first series welcomed, 64/100 by last episode; second compressed, criticised
verdict.note: Wikipedia: 'audience appreciation had by the last episode reached 64 out of 100 from an initial score of 56'; listeners 'enjoyed the first series, where Tiller had followed Tolkien's advice to make a selection of scenes and cut the rest. They were far more critical of the second series, where Tiller had compressed many scenes, resulting in what a self-described "Civil Servant" called "a footling and ridiculous sounding adventure story"'. Two caveats short of VERBATIM: 64 is the last-episode score (initial 56), and the footling phrase is one named listener's, quoted by the page as the result of the compression, not a general verdict.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the general verdict - 'a footling and ridiculous sounding adventure story' is one named listener's phrase, quoted as the result of the compression

claim: Tolkien described Norman Shelley's Bombadil as dreadful and the announcer's misdescription of Goldberry and Willowman as worse still (Letters 175, 176, 198).
source: Stuart D. Lee, 'A Milestone in BBC History? The 1955-56 Radio Dramatization of The Lord of the Rings' (Oxford ORA)
quote: dreadful

verdict.trueWording: Bombadil 'dreadful'; Goldberry/Willowman description 'worse still'
verdict.note: Raw PDF footnote 2: Letters #175 (Molly Waldron 30/11/55) carries both quotes; the same footnote cites Letters #176 and #198. Note: #176/#198 are cited as further references, not as the source of the two quoted phrases.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the citation of Letters #176 and #198, which are cited on the page as further references, not as the source of the two quoted phrases

claim: The 2017 Tolkien: Medieval and Modern post argues Jackson replaced Tolkien's speech-register distinctions (rustic hobbits, more antique Gondor and Rohan) with visual accents, turning Gandalf's conditional syntax into the flat 'The Ring is altogether evil'.
source: How Peter Jackson's Movies Fail to Adapt Tolkien's Style (Tolkien: Medieval and Modern, 2017)
quote: The Ring is altogether evil

verdict.trueWording: Post says Jackson uses accents 'immersing them in the sounds'
verdict.note: Register limbs all verbatim: Appendix F 'hobbits indeed spoke for the most part a rustic dialect, whereas in Gondor and Rohan a more antique language was used'; 'Jackson uses accents to convey these differences instead'; the conditional-syntax contrast and the film line 'The Ring is altogether evil' are both on the page (dated April 11, 2017).
verdict.unsupportedLimb: Accents called 'visual' - the post treats accents as auditory ('immersing them in the sounds of Middle Earth'), explicitly distinct from the films' visuals

claim: Kullmann and Siepmann's corpus study shows Aragorn archaic with inversions, Sam colloquial and politely hedged, Gandalf plain and commanding, Legolas and Gimli proverbial, and Gollum an idiolect of obsessive repetition and minimal syntax.
source: Tolkien's prose style (Wikipedia)

verdict.trueWording: Gollum's 'extraordinary idiolect' is Rosebury's phrase, not theirs
verdict.note: The Fellowship table 'after Kullmann and Siepmann' supports five limbs exactly: Aragorn Archaic/literary with Inversion; Sam Colloquial, rustic, working class, 'Often politely hedged'; Gandalf Plain, flexible, Commands; Gimli and Legolas Literary with Proverbs. Kullmann and Siepmann's corpus linguistics is also stated. But Gollum is outside the table and outside their attribution.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: Gollum's idiolect of obsessive repetition and minimal syntax - the page attributes that to Brian Rosebury; Kullmann and Siepmann are cited only for Gollum's 'non-standard speech'

claim: Turner shows Tolkien's paratactic 'and'-linked sentences at key moments create an impression of exalted register through biblical association without archaic vocabulary.
source: Tolkien's prose style (Wikipedia)
quote: an impression of exalted register

verdict.trueWording: readers experience it as 'an impression of exalted register'
verdict.note: Raw Wikipedia text: Turner on the Pelennor eucatastrophe passage - paratactic style with repeated 'and' 'in the manner of the New Testament', the impression arising 'because of the biblical association'; Turner's 'special stylistic effects at key moments' supports the key-moments limb. The page says Tolkien uses 'few unusual or archaic words' there rather than none.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'no archaic words' - the page says Tolkien uses 'few unusual or archaic words' in the passage, not none

claim: The Silmarillion documents events briefly as if in annals rather than describing persons, giving what Shippey calls more rarefied air.
source: Tolkien's prose style (Wikipedia)
quote: more rarefied air

verdict.trueWording: "more rarefied air" (Shippey, quoted verbatim on the page)
verdict.note: Section 'The Silmarillion': 'The Silmarillion, by contrast with The Lord of the Rings, is written in a compressed style, in which events are briefly documented as if in annals recording history and legend, rather than described with much focus on persons or the niceties of conventional storytelling' (attributed to Bratman); the next sentence: 'Shippey states that The Silmarillion comes across to the reader as a more distant and mythic work ... there was in his view no place for humorously earthy Hobbits in the "more rarefied air" of that work.' Quote verbatim and both factual limbs present; the claim's connective 'giving' joins two adjacent, same-subject sentences by different scholars (Bratman for the annals limb, Shippey for the phrase) rather than reproducing a stated causal link.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the causal connective 'giving' - the page joins two adjacent sentences by different scholars (Bratman for the annals, Shippey for 'more rarefied air') without asserting the link

claim: Stimpson accused Tolkien of shunning ordinary diction and Moorcock called the style comforting and unchallenging, charges Rosebury refuted by showing plain modern English.
source: Tolkien's prose style (Wikipedia)
quote: ordinary diction

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that Rosebury refuted Moorcock's charge — the page ties Rosebury's reply only to Stimpson's attack, never to Moorcock
verdict.trueWording: Rosebury 'systematically replies to each item in Stimpson's attack'
verdict.note: Quote verbatim and the two accusations are exact. Lead and 'Criticism' section: Stimpson 'wrote in 1969 that Tolkien not only "shun[s] ordinary diction, he also wrenches syntax"'; 'In 1978 ... Michael Moorcock, in his essay Epic Pooh, criticized Tolkien for utilizing a comforting and unchallenging writing style'. Rosebury limb: 'The scholar of humanities Brian Rosebury systematically replies to each item in Stimpson's attack, showing that Tolkien mostly uses plain modern English.' The page confines Rosebury's rebuttal to Stimpson; the claim's plural 'charges Rosebury refuted' extends it to Moorcock, which the page does not support. Note also the page says 'mostly uses plain modern English'.

claim: Rosebury shows Tolkien favours familiar phrasal verbs such as 'have on' and 'get off' over the more literary 'wear' and 'dismount'.
source: Tolkien: A Cultural Phenomenon (Wikipedia)
quote: familiar phrasal verbs

verdict.trueWording: "familiar phrasal verbs 'have on' and 'get off'" vs "'wear' and 'dismount'"
verdict.note: Raw wikitext of en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolkien:_A_Cultural_Phenomenon fetched with a browser UA via ?action=raw. Reception section: 'Allan Turner comments in the same work that Rosebury rejects the unsupported assertions of archaising and "wrenched syntax" by critics like Catharine Stimpson, and that Rosebury pointed out that Tolkien used a plain descriptive style, demonstrably favouring the "familiar phrasal verbs 'have on' and 'get off' .. to the slightly more literary 'wear' and 'dismount'".' Quote verbatim; every limb supported. Only difference is intensity: the page reads 'slightly more literary', the claim 'the more literary'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the dropped hedge - the page reads 'slightly more literary', not 'the more literary'
